Article Title: Mumbai-bound traffic hit after hatchback catches fire on Vashi Creek bridge
Article Text:
The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine.





NAVI MUMBAI: Vehicular traffic from Navi Mumbai towards Mumbai was disrupted for around 30 minutes after a hatchback caught fire while crossing the Vashi Creek Bridge on Friday at around 7.30pm.The driver escaped unhurt. He immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. However, the fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred.Vashi traffic police alerted the Vashi fire brigade, which reached the spot within 15 minutes. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.Sunil Kadam, senior inspector of the Vashi traffic unit, said the driver was identified as Sumit Bhikaji Kadam.“At around 7.45pm, we received a call from one Rahul, whose full name is not known, informing us that a car had caught fire on the Mumbai-bound lane of the Vashi Creek Bridge,” said AV Sisode, the on-duty fireman at Vashi fire station.“In the meantime, we also received a call from the Vashi traffic police and immediately rushed to the spot with a fire tender. The Mumbai fire brigade team had also reached the spot as there was some confusion over the jurisdiction,” Sisode said.The fire was subsequently extinguished, and the Vashi fire brigade team returned to the station at around 8.30pm.
Article Summary: The driver immediately pulled the car over to the roadside after noticing smoke emanating from the engine. The fire soon engulfed the entire vehicle, leaving it completely charred. The charred vehicle was later towed away by a crane, following which traffic movement returned to normal.

Article Title: Video: Man sleeps atop 100-ft canopy overnight at Thane station, commuters mistake him for dead
Article Text:
Amidst the morning rush at Thane railway station, chaos ensued when a man was spotted sleeping atop a towering 100-foot canopy





THANE: A man who climbed a 100-foot-high Satis canopy outside Thane railway station and slept on top of it since the previous night triggered panic among early morning commuters, who mistook him for a body and alerted the authorities. Rescue teams eventually allayed their fears and brought him down safely after an hour-long operation.Passengers heading towards the bus station were in for an unusual sight when they spotted what appeared to be a body lying motionless on the semi-transparent canopy. They immediately alerted the police and fire brigade. Rescue personnel, however, struggled to reach the top of the canopy, which has no direct access route. Meanwhile, a crowd gathered on the elevated deck as teams worked out a way to bring the man down.“Rescue personnel managed to climb up to the metal ring supporting the canopy but could not reach the spot where the man was lying. Fortunately, the commotion woke him up. We persuaded him to carefully slide down the arched support to the ring, from where our team brought him down safely. One wrong move could have resulted in a fatal fall onto the deck or the auto stand below from a height of nearly 100 feet,” said a policeman at the spot.Yasin Tadvi, in-charge of the Regional Disaster Management Cell (RDMC), said authorities were investigating how the man managed to climb the structure without any support.The man, who was reportedly neither under the influence of alcohol nor mentally unstable, was later handed over to Thane Nagar police for further investigation. Preliminary information revealed that he had migrated from Amravati and was staying with his wife and child at Thane railway station.“Why he climbed the canopy remains unclear,” an official said.Meanwhile, commuters urged the authorities to take preventive measures to ensure there was no repeat of such an incident, which they said could also prove fatal.
Article Summary: A man climbed a 100-foot-high Satis canopy outside Thane railway station and slept on top of it since the previous night. Early morning commuters mistook him for a body and alerted the authorities. Rescue teams eventually allayed their fears and brought him down safely after an hour-long operation.

Article Title: 'Hum ab nahi aayenge': Drought strain on migrant workers in Pune, many head home
Article Text:
Migrant workers queue up at Pune station to board a train

Hum ab nahi aayenge

Aab agle saal Dilli jayenge, ya phir Mumbai

He says, “Bihar ke log himmat nahi haarte

Bihar mein abhi bhi bahaar hai (job scenario hasn’t changed there yet),”

Kaam se nikal diya hai toh kya kare

Kaam humko mil jayega kahi bhi





PUNE: This festive season, several migrant workers from Bihar earning a living in the city will head home forever — jobless under the cascading effect of drought in Maharashtra.A heavy rush of home-bound workers at Pune Junction station before Diwali and Chhath is common. What’s out of syllabus this time is the anxiety among migrant workers instead of the festive joy. The “out-of-job” remorse is unmistakable. But none curses former employers replacing them with drought-hit relatives and friends. Rational “jobless” migrant workers do understand the “crisis”.Dinu Kumar (40), hailing from Supaul district in Bihar, stands in a serpentine queue on platform number 1 after losing his job at an automobile repair shop in Nigdi. “I have been fixing tyres for the past two years.(I will not come back now),” he says.“My employer recently hired three men from Beed — relatives of one of his acquaintances. He told me that they were farm workers. They lost their livelihoods because of drought. My employer could not turn them away. I tried explaining that I had the necessary experience, but he did not change his decision.(Next year, I will go to Delhi or Mumbai),” Dinu says, without disclosing if he was compensated for the job loss.Drought-hit farm workers are increasingly moving to cities in search of work. Some of them are being hired as replacements for migrant workers from other states keen to go home during festival time.Giridhar Paswan (46) from Madhubani district becomes anxious at the sight of RPF personnel, some accompanied by sniffer dogs, patrolling the crowded platform. “Why do they think we are criminals? We are hardworking men,” he quips.Giridhar says, “I worked as an eatery waiter and security guard in Pimpri for a year. My manager told me not to report for work until July next year, citing the need to accommodate a relative affected by drought. He said he would call me when things improved. But how can I wait that long?”(People from Bihar do not lose courage). I will venture out again and find work somewhere.”Hundreds wait anxiously in the holding area of Pune Junction station as Azad Hind Express chugs into platform 1 around 7.40pm on Thursday. Rakesh Mahto (35), a resident of Jehanabad district in Bihar, wants to board the train to Kolkata after losing his security guard’s job at a commercial complex in Hadapsar.“I worked there for over two years before being removed last month without an explanation. I later learnt that someone from Nanded was hired in my place. Diwali and Chhath will mean little unless I have a job. A friend has promised to help me find work in Kolkata, so I am heading there,” he says.Why not Bihar? “Rakesh quips.The jobless migrant workers’ absence of anger towards former employers springs a surprise. “Circumstances forced their decisions. Better opportunities will come our way,” says Rakesh.The holding area remains stiflingly humid despite several ceiling fans. RPF personnel pull up a large group of passengers for attempting to break the queue. Hira Singh (43), a mason from Katihar district, tries to explain to an officer that he had mistaken the platform of Pune-Supaul Express.(What can I do if I have been removed from work)? I had been working as a mason for three years. I am going home because my elderly mother’s last wish is to celebrate Chhath with me.(I will get work somewhere),” Hira says.Not all at the station will head home for good. Ravi Kumar (25) from Vaishali district in Bihar, a security guard at a housing society in Koregaon Park, says, “I just want to spend some quality time with my family. I might even get married this time.”Ravi’s companions in the queue break into laughter.
Article Summary: Drought-hit farm workers are increasingly moving to cities in search of work. Some of them are being hired as replacements for migrant workers from other states keen to go home during festival time. “Circumstances forced their decisions. Better opportunities will come our way,” says Rakesh Mahto.
